title: Hydrotherapy pools: temperature, disinfection and vulnerable users
audience: Trained pool technicians and operators servicing public hydrotherapy pools in SA, where users may be injured, unwell or immune-compromised. Figures apply under the state standard.
learningOutcomes: State the temperature, humidity and disinfectant requirements for a hydrotherapy pool.
Explain why hydrotherapy pools need a higher disinfectant level than ordinary pools.
Describe the supervision and exclusion points that protect vulnerable users.

instruction.heading: Why hydrotherapy pools run differently
instruction.body: Hydrotherapy pools run at a higher temperature and need a higher disinfectant level, because warm water accelerates the loss of disinfectant. They serve people rehabilitating after injury or sickness, people whose immune systems are weakened, and people with intellectual impairment, plus people who exercise there. Because of these users, the standard treats running a hydrotherapy pool as work needing extra care.

instruction.heading: Temperature and air conditions
instruction.body: Hydrotherapy water should stay at or below 38 degrees Celsius, with 28 to 35 degrees as the aim. The thermostat must hold the set temperature within 0.5 degrees either way, and an over-temperature alarm must be fitted to warn above 38 degrees. Air in the pool zone should sit within 10 degrees below the water, and humidity should stay between 50 and 75 percent, with draughts kept down.

instruction.heading: Turnover, replacement and disinfectant
instruction.body: The full pool volume has to be filtered no less often than every two hours, and under an hour is suggested for busy pools. For heavy bather loads, the standard recommends replacing about a quarter of the water each week. Free chlorine must be at least 2.0 mg/L, and under heavy loads at high temperature the standard suggests at least 4.0 mg/L. For bromine, the minimum is 4.0 mg/L, with 8.0 mg/L suggested when the water is hot and heavily loaded.

instruction.heading: Stabilisers and microbial growth
instruction.body: Stabilisers are barred from indoor hydrotherapy water, and the standard discourages them in outdoor water as well. Warm water and a heavy organic load make these pools a favourable home for microbes, so a fast-acting disinfectant is the right choice.

instruction.heading: Supervision and exclusions
instruction.body: The standard suggests trained staff supervise users constantly, and that people with impairments get special arrangements. Some medical conditions rule out hydrotherapy, including unstable heart conditions, active infections and open wounds. Users should be supervised, and the operator must have a way to refuse entry where a user is not suitable. Hydrotherapy pool use by people living with HIV carries no risk that can be measured for other users when the pool is properly disinfected and supervised.

procedure: Check the water temperature is within the 28 to 35 degree ideal, below the 38 degree limit, and the alarm works.
Check the air warmth and humidity against the standard's limits.
Test free chlorine or bromine against the hydrotherapy minimums and the higher suggested level for hot, heavily used water.
Confirm the turnover achieved and the weekly replacement record.
Confirm trained supervision is in place before users enter, and that the exclusion process is recorded.

workedExamples.situation: A public hydrotherapy pool reads 36 degrees Celsius and free chlorine at 2.5 mg/L during a busy morning with a full class.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Is the pool compliant, and what must happen?
workedExamples.reasoning: Water at 36 degrees is below the 38 degree limit, so the temperature is acceptable, but it is above the 28 to 35 degree ideal. When the pool is hot and heavily used, the suggested floor is 4.0 mg/L, so 2.5 mg/L falls short. Escalate to the operator, increase the disinfectant as the plan sets, and confirm supervision is in place.

equipmentAndPpe: Calibrated thermometer and hygrometer for pool and air conditions
Free chlorine or bromine and pH test kit
Record sheet for supervision and exclusions

commonErrors.error: Running a hydrotherapy pool at spa temperatures.
commonErrors.prevention: Hydrotherapy water must not go above 38 degrees; the ideal is 28 to 35 degrees.

commonErrors.error: Accepting the minimum disinfectant level on a busy day.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the recommended higher level for upper-temperature heavy use.

commonErrors.error: Using stabilisers because the water feels warm.
commonErrors.prevention: Stabilisers are barred from indoor hydrotherapy pools.

commonErrors.error: Admitting a user with an open wound or acute infection.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse entry under the exclusion rules and record the refusal.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Users may be injured, unwell or immune-compromised. Constant supervision is recommended by the standard, and exclusions must be applied.
Heater, pump and dosing equipment work is licensed where a licence applies. Isolate and lock out before inspection. This lesson does not grant a licence.
Chlorine, bromine and stabilisers are chemicals with safety data sheets. Keep them separated from incompatible products.
Figures are South Australian standard values (revised 2013). Confirm the current regulation text.

qualityStandard: Water temperature, air temperature and humidity are recorded against the standard's limits.
Disinfectant readings are compared with the minimum and with the recommended level for heavy use.
Supervision and exclusions are recorded for every session.
documentationEvidence: Hydrotherapy daily record with temperature, air conditions, disinfectant, pH and turnover
Weekly replacement record and session supervision and exclusion record
summary: Hydrotherapy water stays at or below 38 degrees Celsius, with an ideal of 28 to 35 degrees.
Free chlorine at least 2.0 mg/L, with 4.0 mg/L recommended under heavy upper-temperature use; bromine at least 4.0 mg/L.
Supervise users, apply exclusions, and keep stabilisers out of indoor hydrotherapy pools.
